analysis.one_liner: Rolls back major Wall Street rules from the 2010 Dodd-Frank law and weakens the consumer financial watchdog.
analysis.headline: The House Financial Services Committee passed the bill 30–26 and sent it to the House floor on December 20, 2016, but the 114th Congress ended on January 3, 2017 without a House vote.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill unwinds large pieces of the 2010 Dodd-Frank law passed after the 2008 financial crisis. Banks that hold at least 10% of their assets in reserve could opt out of most federal capital, liquidity, and stress-test rules. It repeals the Volcker Rule, which stops banks from speculating with their own money; repeals the limit on debit card swipe fees; ends the FDIC's process for winding down failing giant banks; strips regulators' power to label firms "too big to fail"; and restructures the Consumer Financial Protection Bureau so it can no longer self-fund, is run by a commission instead of one director, and loses its power to act on "abusive" practices and to restrict forced arbitration. It also repeals the Labor Department rule requiring retirement advisers to act in customers' best interest.
analysis.who_benefits: Large banks and financial firms benefit most: the bill lets them opt out of capital and liquidity standards, removes restrictions on speculative trading and mergers, frees them to charge higher debit card fees, ends mandatory arbitration limits, and removes private reporting requirements for private equity fund advisers. Payday lenders gain a five-year exemption from federal payday lending rules. Broker-dealers gain from repeal of the fiduciary rule for retirement advice. Community banks and credit unions also get genuine relief from reporting and examination burdens.

how_it_helps.text: A bank that maintains a 10% leverage ratio can elect to be exempt from federal capital and liquidity rules, limits on capital distributions, and Dodd-Frank stress-test and systemic-risk standards, and is deemed "well capitalized" [S4].
The bill repeals the Volcker Rule restricting banks' speculative investments and the Durbin Amendment limiting debit card processing fees charged to retailers [S2].

It eliminates the FDIC's orderly liquidation authority for failing financial firms and replaces it with a new bankruptcy process, and removes the Financial Stability Oversight Council's power to designate non-bank firms as systemically important, retroactively repealing past designations [S2].

It replaces the Consumer Financial Protection Bureau's director with a bipartisan commission, subjects the bureau to the congressional appropriations process, limits its authority over "abusive" practices, and repeals its authority to restrict arbitration [S2].

It increases civil penalties for securities-law violations and directs some monetary sanctions to victim relief, and adds mandatory training for financial firms to report suspected financial abuse of seniors ("Senior Safe") [S4].
It provides relief for community institutions, including a short-form call report, extended credit union examination cycles, and a safe harbor for loans held in portfolio [S4].

analysis.who_pays: Consumers and investors bear the costs: higher debit swipe fees would likely be passed through to shoppers; removing the retirement-advice fiduciary rule permits conflicted advice and higher fees for savers; weakening the consumer bureau's funding, structure, and "abusive"-practice authority reduces enforcement against predatory lending and forced arbitration clauses; and removing the orderly liquidation process and "too big to fail" designations leaves fewer tools to contain a failing giant bank, raising the risk that a future failure spreads losses to the wider economy and taxpayers.

drawbacks.text: Repealing the Durbin Amendment would allow banks to charge retailers higher debit card interchange fees, a cost likely passed to consumers through prices [S2].

Repealing the FDIC's orderly liquidation authority removes the mechanism used to wind down a failing systemically important firm without disorderly collapse; the replacement bankruptcy process is untested for firms of that scale [S2].

Restructuring the Consumer Financial Protection Bureau, subjecting it to yearly appropriations, and removing its "abusive"-practice and arbitration-restriction authorities would reduce enforcement against predatory lending and forced arbitration clauses [S2].
Repealing the Labor Department's fiduciary rule ends the requirement that brokers managing retirement money act in the customer's best interest [S4].

Supporters' strongest good-faith case is the trade-off the bill itself builds in: banks must hold a full 10% of assets as equity — roughly double current requirements — to get the deregulatory election, which backers argue makes banks safer even with fewer rules; an honest supporter would also concede that repealing the orderly liquidation authority, retroactively undoing "too big to fail" designations, and weakening the consumer bureau all increase the chance that problems resurface only after losses are incurred [S4].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill bundles some genuinely useful provisions — community bank reporting relief, higher securities-fraud penalties, senior financial abuse training, and small-business capital formation changes — inside a framework whose main effect is to lift oversight off the largest financial firms. For ordinary people, the dominant effects are negative: more risk carried by taxpayers, higher swipe fees, weaker consumer enforcement, and conflicted retirement advice. The few protections it adds do not offset the scale of what it removes from the post-2008 regulatory framework.

outcome.mechanism: The House Financial Services Committee passed it 30–26 in September 2016, the full House never voted on it, and the 114th Congress ended on January 3, 2017 with the bill sitting on the House calendar.

narrative.text: Rep. Jeb Hensarling introduced the Financial CHOICE Act of 2016 in the House on September 9, 2016, with five Republican cosponsors [S1].
The House Financial Services Committee considered and marked up the bill on September 13, 2016, and ordered it reported by a vote of 30–26 [S6].

On December 20, 2016, the committee reported the bill amended, seven other committees were discharged, and the bill was placed on the Union Calendar, meaning it was eligible for a House floor vote [S3, S6].
No House floor vote ever occurred, and the 114th Congress ended on January 3, 2017, so the bill died without a vote in either chamber [S1, S6].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Because the bill died without a floor vote, the post-2008 financial rules it targeted — the Volcker Rule, the FDIC liquidation authority, the consumer bureau's funding and authorities, and the debit fee cap — all remained in force at the end of the 114th Congress, while large banks and other financial firms were denied the deregulatory relief the bill would have delivered.

for.name: Rep. Jeb Hensarling
for.role: Chair, House Financial Services Committee; bill sponsor
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and, as committee chair, brought it through a 30–26 committee markup and reported it to the House floor in December 2016.

for.name: House Financial Services Committee Republicans
for.what_they_did: Voted 30–26 in committee to order the bill reported amended to the House floor.

for.name: Large banks and financial industry trade groups
for.what_they_did: Supported the bill's agenda of repealing Dodd-Frank provisions on capital standards, the Volcker Rule, the debit fee cap, and consumer bureau authority.

against.name: House Financial Services Committee Democrats
against.what_they_did: Voted no in the committee markup, producing the 30–26 vote that reported the bill.

against.name: Obama administration
against.what_they_did: Opposed legislation unwinding the Dodd-Frank Act's bank regulations and consumer protections.

against.name: House leadership of the 114th Congress
against.what_they_did: Never brought the bill to the House floor for a vote before the Congress ended on January 3, 2017.

sides.party_line_note: The bill was sponsored and cosponsored only by Republicans, and it cleared the Financial Services Committee on a 30–26 vote in which Republicans supplied the 30 votes in favor and Democrats the 26 against.

industries.industry: Large banks and diversified financial firms
industries.note: Banks holding a 10% leverage ratio could opt out of capital, liquidity, and stress-test rules; the Volcker Rule ban on speculative trading would be repealed; and firms would lose "systemically important" designations and the FDIC's wind-down process. The public bears the added risk that a future failure spreads into a broader crisis or taxpayer rescue [S2, S4].

industries.industry: Consumer financial firms, including payday lenders
industries.note: The bill gives state and tribal payday lenders a five-year exemption from consumer bureau rules and strips the bureau's authority to act on "abusive" practices, restricting the main federal cop on the beat for predatory lending [S2, S4].
Repealing the Labor Department fiduciary rule ends the requirement that advisers act in retirement savers' best interest, permitting conflicted advice and higher fees [S4].

industries.industry: Debit card issuers and payment networks
industries.note: Repealing the Durbin Amendment removes the cap on debit swipe fees charged to retailers, a cost that flows to merchants and then to consumers through prices [S2].
The bill exempts private equity fund advisers from risk-retention, recordkeeping, and reporting requirements, reducing transparency available to investors [S4].

These institutions get real, targeted relief — short-form call reports, longer examination cycles, portfolio-loan safe harbors, and access to the same capital election as big banks — which lowers their compliance costs; the risk trade-offs sit mainly with the largest firms, not them [S4].
Repealing the Durbin Amendment exposes retailers to unlimited debit interchange fees, directly reversing a protection for merchants and the shoppers who ultimately pay the fees [S2].
